solution:
Section 15.3.5 opens with the statement that polyamide polymers are generally known as nylons, and that they are the linear polyamides obtained by condensation of dicarboxylic acids with diamines, by self condensation of an amino acid, or by ring opening polymerization of lactams. Nylon fibres are therefore polyamide fibres, and section 15.3.5 adds that the inter unit linkage in them is the amide group \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\).

The other three are excluded by the chapter's own definitions. Semisynthetic fibres are the regenerated cellulose derivatives of section 15.2.1 (cellulose acetate rayon, cellulose nitrate, viscose rayon, cuprammonium rayon); nylon is listed there under synthetic polymers, not semisynthetic. Polyester fibres are joined by the ester link \(\mathrm{-C(=O)-O-}\) and are represented by terylene or dacron in section 15.3.6, which is a different linkage from the amide link. Cellulose fibres are the plant polymers of section 15.2.1, such as cotton and linen.

Hence nylon fibres are polyamide fibres.

Section 15.2.1 classifies polymers by source into natural, synthetic and semisynthetic. Natural polymers are obtained from plant sources (cotton, linen, natural rubber) or animal sources (wool, silk), and section 15.1 names proteins among the important naturally occurring organic biopolymers. Protein is therefore the naturally occurring polymer in this list.

Each of the other three is man made. Teflon is polytetrafluoroethylene, prepared in section 15.3.3 by polymerising tetrafluoroethylene with a free radical initiator. Polyethylene is prepared in section 15.3.2 from ethylene under high pressure or over a Ziegler-Natta catalyst. PVC appears in Table 15.1 as the polymer of vinyl chloride. All three belong to the synthetic class of section 15.2.1.

Hence the naturally occurring polymer here is protein.

Under natural polymers, section 15.2.1 separates plant polymers from animal polymers and states that silk is obtained from the silkworm. Silk is therefore an animal fibre.

The other three options name the categories the chapter assigns elsewhere. A semisynthetic fibre is a regenerated cellulose derivative such as viscose rayon or acetate rayon; a synthetic fibre is a man made polymer such as nylon, terylene or neoprene; and a vegetable or plant fibre is one obtained from a plant, such as the cotton and linen named in the same section. Silk is none of these, since it comes from a living animal and is not manufactured or chemically modified.

Hence silk is an animal fibre.

Section 15.3.6 states that the commercially most important polyester fibre is terylene, also called dacron, obtained by condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid. Dacron is therefore another name for terylene.

The other three names belong to different polymers in the same chapter. Nylon 6 is the polyamide made in section 15.3.5 by ring opening polymerization of \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam. Orlon is the fibre made from polyacrylonitrile in section 15.3.4. Novolac is the phenol-formaldehyde moulding powder formed in the first two stages of bakelite manufacture in section 15.3.7.

Hence dacron is another name of terylene.

Section 15.3.5 states that the polyamide polymers are generally known as nylons and that they contain \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) groups as the inter unit linkages. Nylon is therefore the polymer made up of polyamides.

Dacron is ruled out because section 15.3.6 identifies it as terylene, a polyester whose repeating units are joined by an ester link, not an amide link. Rayon is ruled out because section 15.2.1 places the rayons among the semisynthetic regenerated cellulose derivatives. Jute is a natural plant fibre, that is a cellulose material of the kind section 15.2.1 lists under plant polymers, and carries no amide linkage.

Hence nylon is the one made up of polyamides.

Section 15.3.5 shows \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam as a cyclic amide, that is a lactam, whose ring opens on heating with water to give nylon 6 with the repeating unit \(\mathrm{[NH-(CH_2)_5-CO]_n}\). Reading the ring back from that repeating unit, it is built from one nitrogen atom, one carbonyl carbon and five \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups. The number of carbon atoms in the ring is therefore \(1 + 5 = 6\), which is exactly why the chapter says the name nylon 6 is given on the basis of the six carbon atoms present in the monomer unit.

Five undercounts, because it takes the five \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups and omits the carbonyl carbon. Two is far too small for a seven membered lactam ring. Seven is the total number of atoms in the ring, six carbons plus the one nitrogen, so it answers ring SIZE rather than the carbon count the question asks for.

Hence \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam has six carbon atoms in its ring.

Section 15.3.6 introduces the polyesters as the polymers having an ester linkage joining the repeating units, and names terylene, also called dacron, as the commercially most important polyester fibre, made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid.

A polyamide fibre is excluded because that class is the nylons of section 15.3.5, joined by \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) links rather than ester links. A vegetable fibre is excluded because that is a plant polymer such as cotton or linen from section 15.2.1, whereas terylene is man made. A protein fibre is excluded for the same reason, protein being the animal biopolymer of section 15.1 and not a laboratory condensation product.

Hence terylene is a polyester fibre.

Section 15.3.6 states that PET is another trade name of the polyester polyethyleneterephthalate, and that this polyester is obtained by condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, the reaction eliminating \(n\,\mathrm{H_2O}\) as the ester links are formed.

Addition is excluded by the definition in section 15.2.3, where addition polymerization proceeds without loss of any small molecule and requires monomers containing a double bond; PET loses water and neither of its monomers is an alkene. Alkylation and hydration are not modes of polymerization at all: section 15.2.3 lists only addition, condensation and ring opening polymerization.

Hence PET is formed by condensation.

Section 15.2.1 lists cotton among the plant polymers obtained directly from the cotton plant, and section 15.3.10 states that cellulose is a linear polymer of glucose units with molecular formula \(\mathrm{(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n}\). Chemically pure cotton is therefore cellulose itself.

The other three are cellulose DERIVATIVES rather than cellulose. Section 15.2.1 groups acetate rayon and cellulose nitrate with the semisynthetic polymers, that is polymers derived from a natural polymer by chemical modification. Viscose rayon is treated in section 15.3.10, where cellulose is converted through alkali cellulose and cellulose xanthate and then regenerated, so it is processed rather than pure natural material.

Hence chemically pure cotton is cellulose.

Section 15.3.3 describes teflon as polytetrafluoroethylene, \(\mathrm{[CF_2-CF_2]_n}\), and states directly that the C-F bond is very difficult to break and remains unaffected by corrosive alkali and organic solvents. Its chemical inertness is therefore due to the C-F bond.

A C-H bond cannot be responsible, because every hydrogen of ethylene has been replaced by fluorine in tetrafluoroethylene, so the polymer contains no C-H bond at all. Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force of the kind discussed in section 15.2.4, which governs mechanical properties such as tensile strength rather than resistance to chemical attack, and teflon has no hydrogen to donate. A C=C bond is absent as well, since the monomer's double bond is consumed during addition polymerization to give a saturated backbone; a residual double bond would in any case make the polymer more reactive, not less.

Hence teflon is chemically inert due to the presence of the C-F bond.
